Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the AeroSpace Dynamics Inc. Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. As a reminder, instructions for queuing up will be given at that time. Please note this event is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Mike Chen, Vice President of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Mike Chen:
Thank you, Operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to AeroSpace Dynamics Inc.'s Q2 2024 Earnings Conference Call. Joining me today are Alex Thompson, Chief Executive Officer; John Ramirez, Chief Financial Officer; and Sarah Patel, Chief Operating Officer.

Before we begin, I'd like to remind you that this call contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995. Please refer to our SEC filings, including our most recent Form 10-K and 10-Q, for a complete discussion of risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those discussed today.

Alex Thompson:
Thank you, Mike, and good morning. AeroSpace Dynamics delivered a solid performance in Q2, demonstrating the resilience of our business model and the strength of our diversified portfolio across defense, commercial aviation, and space. Our priorities remain focused on executing our strategy, driving operational excellence, and delivering value to our shareholders. Today, I'll cover our key operational highlights, including the analysis of our revenue drivers and headwinds, the strong momentum in aftermarket and services revenue growth, our updated revenue and earnings guidance for the full year, and our R&D investments in next-generation platforms and technologies.

We are particularly excited about the recent advancements in our hypersonic glide vehicle program and its potential to drive multi-year revenue growth through low-rate initial production ramps. We are seeing strong demand for our defense systems, bolstered by geopolitical tensions, and our commercial aerospace business is recovering steadily with robust aftermarket tailwinds.

With that, I'll turn it over to John to walk through the financial details.

John Ramirez:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Today, I'd like to dive deeper into our Q2 results, specifically the key revenue drivers that propelled us to $8.2 billion in top-line growth—up 12% year-over-year and 5% sequentially—and the headwinds we're navigating as we execute on our multi-year growth strategy at AeroSpace Dynamics Inc., or ASD.

Our revenue composition remains diversified across our three core segments: Defense Systems at 45% of total revenue, Commercial Aviation at 35%, and Space & Advanced Technologies at 20%. This balance has been a hallmark of our resilience, with a book-to-bill ratio of 1.25x, supporting a record backlog of $145 billion, up 8% from last quarter. 

First, Defense Systems was our standout performer, delivering $3.7 billion in revenue—a robust 18% YoY increase. Geopolitical tensions in Eastern Europe and the Indo-Pacific have accelerated demand for our precision-guided munitions and next-gen platforms. For instance, our hypersonic glide vehicle program, akin to the DARPA-modeled HAWC initiatives, ramped to low-rate initial production ahead of schedule, contributing $450 million this quarter alone. We've secured $2.8 billion in incremental awards from the U.S. DoD's FY24 budget, including a sole-source contract for JASSM-ER integration on F-15EX platforms, mirroring recent Boeing-Lockheed synergies.

Regionally, U.S. government funding remains our bedrock at 60% of segment revenue, bolstered by the $886 billion NDAA authorization. But international sales surged 25% YoY to $1.1 billion, driven by NATO allies like Poland and the UK ramping up F-35 sustainment under the JSF program's Block 4 upgrades. In Asia-Pacific, our partnerships with regional primes—think IAI and Hindustan Aeronautics—yielded a $600 million offset deal for P-8A Poseidon derivatives, capitalizing on maritime domain awareness needs amid South China Sea frictions.

Aftermarket services in Defense added tailwinds, up 22% to $850 million, as fleet utilization rates hit 85% post-Ukraine drawdowns, with MRO demand for our C-130J Hercules upgrades outpacing supply.

Shifting to Commercial Aviation, we posted $2.9 billion, a solid 5% YoY gain despite OEM softness. Engine OEM volumes for our PW1100G geared turbofan family—powering 60% of the A320neo fleet—grew 12% sequentially, supported by Airbus's 753 deliveries YTD, per Cirium data. Our aftermarket services here exploded 30% to $1.2 billion, fueled by a 15% rise in shop visit rates from Pratt & Whitney's high-pressure turbine durability issues, which we've turned into a $500 million revenue opportunity through our certified MRO network.

Sustainability initiatives are a bright spot: Our sustainable flight test module for 100% SAF compatibility on LEAP-1A engines generated $150 million in early commercialization revenue, aligning with ICAO's CORSIA Phase 2 mandates and positioning us ahead of GE and Safran peers.

Finally, Space & Advanced Technologies hit $1.6 billion, up 10% YoY, led by our Orion spacecraft contributions to NASA's Artemis program—$400 million booked this quarter—and a $1.2 billion contract for hypersonic defense satellites under SDA's Tranche 2. Commercial space revenue, including Starlink-like LEO constellations for OneWeb, grew 15%, tapping into the $7 trillion satellite broadband market forecast by NSR Analytics.

That said, we're not immune to industry-wide pressures. Supply chain disruptions shaved 200 basis points off our top-line growth, with titanium forgings from Ukraine/Russia-exposed sources up 40% in cost and lead times stretching to 18 months—echoing Boeing's 737 MAX delays. Labor shortages in our Oklahoma and Alabama facilities constrained capacity by 5%, though our 4% wage inflation hedge via productivity bonuses kept margins intact.

In Commercial, Boeing's 737 production ramp-down to 38/month amid FAA scrutiny created a $250 million OEM shortfall, offset partially by our diversified exposure to Embraer E-Jets and COMAC C919. Engine durability headwinds on GTFs, with 600+ engines inspected YTD per P&W disclosures, delayed 10% of our 2024 deliveries, pressuring working capital.

Regionally, European headwinds from Airbus supply constraints—labor strikes at Spirit AeroSystems—impacted 8% of our nacelle revenue, while China-exposed supply chains added FX volatility, with the USD/CNY at 7.2 eroding 3% of APAC margins.

Strategically, we're leaning into our $1.5 billion R&D investment—12% of revenue—focusing on digital twins for predictive maintenance, reducing unplanned downtime 25% in simulations, and AI-driven directed energy weapons, positioning us for the DoD's $28 billion Replicator initiative. Partnerships like our Raytheon JADC2 integration and Northrop Grumman teaming on NGAD demonstrator de-risk our pipeline.

Now, let's turn to one of our highest-margin and most resilient revenue streams: aftermarket and services, which grew 22% year-over-year to $1.8 billion in the quarter. This marks our 11th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth in this segment, underscoring the durability of our installed base and the strategic investments we've made in digital sustainment capabilities. For context, this represents about 35% of our total revenue mix, up from 28% three years ago, and delivered an incremental margin of over 1,200 basis points above our OEM product sales.

Our commercial services business continues to outperform, fueled by sustained recovery in global flight hours, which are now 15% above 2019 levels per IATA data. Narrowbody platforms like the Boeing 737 MAX and Airbus A320neo family—where we hold leading positions in CFM LEAP-1A/1B engine MRO and nacelle sustainment—drove over 60% of this growth to $1.1 billion, up 28% YoY. Flight hours on these platforms surged 32% YoY, accelerating demand for our time-and-materials work and long-term service agreements.

A key technical enabler here has been our Predictive Health Management platform, powered by AI-driven digital twins and edge computing. We've now deployed it across 4,500+ engines in service, reducing unplanned shop visits by 25% and enabling proactive component swaps—think high-pressure turbine blades and compressor spools. This not only boosted revenue per flight hour by 18% but also improved customer retention to 98%. Regionally, Asia-Pacific was the star, up 45% YoY, driven by fleet expansions at IndiGo, AirAsia, and Lion Air, where we've secured $2.5 billion in new LTSAs over the past year. North America grew 25%, supported by Delta and United's accelerated maintenance cadences amid supply chain normalization, while EMEA lagged at 15% due to lingering engine availability issues at the Airbus A320neo install base.

Defense sustainment grew 15% YoY to $600 million, tempered by lumpy government funding but underpinned by multi-year performance-based logistics contracts. Our F-35 Lightning II wing sustainment for Lockheed Martin and the U.S. Air Force contributed $250 million, up 20%, as the global fleet surpassed 900 aircraft and accumulated 500,000 flight hours. We've leaned into additive manufacturing initiatives, producing 15,000 titanium structural parts last quarter via our qualified DMLS processes, cutting lead times from 18 months to 8 weeks and capturing 30% share in rapid prototyping for Block 4 upgrades.

The Ukraine conflict and Indo-Pacific tensions have accelerated demand for C-130J Hercules and P-8A Poseidon sustainment, with international sales—led by Australia, Japan, and NATO allies—rising 25%. Domestically, the U.S. DoD's FY24 budget emphasis on readiness, with $120 billion allocated to operations and sustainment, positions us well. Margins here expanded 300 basis points to 28%, thanks to our Integrated Sustainment Ecosystem, which integrates AR/VR for field repairs and blockchain for parts provenance, reducing escape rates by 40%.

Space and emerging services grew 35% YoY to $100 million, reflecting our pivot to commercial space. Revenue from Starlink-like satellite constellations and Vulcan Centaur engine MRO for ULA jumped, with a new $500 million, 10-year sustainment deal for hypersonic vehicle test fleets. We're investing $150 million in orbital debris mitigation services using ML-optimized deorbit kits.

Looking forward on aftermarket, we expect full-year growth of 20-23%, with Q3 at the high end, driven by 10% organic flight hour growth and $8 billion in new contract wins YTD—60% multi-year. Risks include FX headwinds in EMEA with the euro down 5% YoY and potential U.S. government shutdown delays, but our 85% backlog visibility mitigates this. Strategically, we're doubling down on totalcare-like bundled offerings, targeting 50% of commercial revenue from fixed-price LTSAs by 2025, akin to Rolls-Royce's model. This shifts us from transactional time-and-materials to annuity-like streams, with ROIC north of 25%.

We've also launched ASD Nexus, a cloud-based MRO marketplace connecting 200+ Tier-1 suppliers, which onboarded 50 new customers this quarter and is already generating $50 million in ecosystem fees. Competitively, this positions us ahead of peers like Honeywell and Pratt & Whitney, who are playing catch-up on digital threads.

I'll now turn to our updated full-year 2024 guidance, which reflects the strong momentum we're seeing across our portfolio amid a resilient macroeconomic backdrop and heightened global defense priorities. As a reminder, back in our Q1 earnings call, we guided for full-year revenue of $18.5 billion to $19.0 billion, with adjusted EPS of $8.50 to $9.00, and segment operating margins in the mid-teens. Today, we're raising that guidance across the board, driven by better-than-expected program execution, backlog conversion, and new award momentum.

Starting with our Commercial Aviation business, which represents about 35% of our mix, we're now expecting revenue of $6.8 billion to $7.2 billion, up from our prior guide of $6.4 billion to $6.8 billion. This reflects robust demand for our next-generation narrowbody platforms, including the ASD A-350X regional jet, where we've seen order intake accelerate 25% year-over-year, fueled by low-cost carrier expansions in Asia-Pacific. Air traffic has rebounded to 105% of 2019 levels globally, per IATA data, and our supply chain optimizations—particularly in titanium forgings and composite structures—have reduced lead times by 18 months on key assemblies. Margins here are tracking toward 12-14%, a 200-basis-point improvement, thanks to productivity gains from our Industry 4.0 digital twin initiatives on the assembly line.

Shifting to Defense & Mission Systems, our largest segment at 45% of revenue, we're raising guidance to $8.7 billion to $9.2 billion, versus $8.3 billion to $8.7 billion previously. This is anchored by a record $25 billion backlog, up 15% year-to-date, with strong contributions from fixed-price development contracts on the NGAD sixth-generation fighter adjunct programs and hypersonic boost-glide vehicles. Geopolitical tensions—Ukraine sustainment needs, Indo-Pacific deterrence, and Middle East ISR requirements—have driven a 30% uptick in U.S. DoD funding for our integrated air defense systems, including the Patriot GEM-T interceptor upgrades we're producing alongside Raytheon. Internationally, NATO allies like Poland and Australia have accelerated F-35 sustainment and electronic warfare pod deliveries, adding $1.2 billion in new awards this quarter alone. We're forecasting segment margins of 16-18%, benefiting from 85% fixed-price contract mix and labor efficiencies from our AI-driven predictive maintenance on C-130J Hercules fleets.

Our Space & Advanced Technologies segment, about 20% of the total, is now guided to $3.7 billion to $4.0 billion, lifted from $3.5 billion to $3.8 billion. Key tailwinds include NASA Artemis contract ramps for Orion crew modules and commercial lunar lander propulsion systems, plus DoD space domain awareness sats in partnership with Northrop Grumman. The proliferation of LEO constellations—think Starshield analogs—has boosted demand for our Hall-effect thrusters and optical comms payloads, with a 40% YoY increase in launch manifests. Margins here expand to 14-16%, supported by reusable rocket tech transfers from our hypersonic testbed programs.

On a consolidated basis, we're updating full-year revenue guidance to $19.2 billion to $20.0 billion, implying 8-12% growth at the midpoint and accelerating to 15% organically excluding FX. Adjusted diluted EPS is now $9.20 to $9.80, up from $8.50-$9.00, with the raise driven by 150 basis points of margin expansion to 14.5-15.5% overall, lower interest expense from our recent $500 million debt refinancing at 4.2%, and a 10 million share share repurchase authorization. Free cash flow remains targeted at $1.8 billion to $2.0 billion, or 10% of revenue, funding $400 million in R&D for directed energy weapons and sustainable aviation fuels—critical for FAA NextGen compliance and DoD's Replicator initiative.

Regionally, North America stays dominant at 65% of revenue, but we're seeing APAC grow to 20% from 17%, on AUKUS submarine combat systems and Japanese F-X fighter workshares. EMEA is flat at 12% amid UK Tempest program delays, offset by Saudi offset deals. Supply chain risks are mitigated; we've diversified 70% of rare earths away from China via U.S. domestic sourcing partnerships.

Strategically, this guidance embeds our focus on high-margin IDIQ vehicles like JADC2 and GBSD ground systems, where we hold 25% market share. We're prioritizing capital returns—dividend up 10% this year—while investing in dual-use tech like quantum-resistant encryption for both Boeing 787 avionics and B-21 Raider networks. Risks remain around labor shortages in precision machining and potential sequestration, but our 2.5x book-to-bill and $32 billion five-year backlog provide strong visibility.

Before I move on, I'd like to spend a few minutes on our R&D investments in next-generation platforms and technologies, as this remains a cornerstone of our long-term growth strategy in the Aerospace & Defense sector. We operate in an industry where technological superiority directly translates to mission success and contract wins, especially amid escalating great-power competition with near-peers like China and Russia.

In Q2 alone, we deployed $2.8 billion in R&D spend, bringing our year-to-date total to $7.9 billion—up 18% year-over-year and tracking toward our full-year guidance of $10.5 billion, or approximately 4.7% of projected revenues. This represents a deliberate ramp-up in R&D intensity from 3.9% in FY2021 to our current levels, outpacing the industry average of around 4.2% as reported in Deloitte's latest A&D sector benchmarking study. We're funding this through a balanced mix: roughly 45% Independent Research and Development from our cash flows—bolstered by strong FCF generation of $3.2 billion YTD—and 55% customer-funded Contract Research and Development from primes like the U.S. DoD's Science and Technology Reinvestment budget, which saw a 12% uplift in the FY2024 NDAA to $14.5 billion.

First, next-generation air dominance platforms account for 38% of our R&D allocation or about $4 billion annually. We're heavily invested in the Next Generation Air Dominance family of systems, including digital prototypes for the crewed fighter and attritable Collaborative Combat Aircraft. In Q2, we achieved a major milestone with our NGAD Risk Reduction prototype, demonstrating Mach 2+ supercruise with adaptive cycle engines derived from GE's XA102 and Pratt & Whitney's XA103 technologies. This positions us favorably for the anticipated $20 billion NGAD PEN contract expected in FY2025. We've also integrated AI-driven autonomy stacks, leveraging our Model-Based Systems Engineering toolchain to compress the design cycle by 30%, from traditional 10-year timelines to under 7 years.

Hypersonics and missile technologies represent 27% of spend, or $2.8 billion FY guidance. Here, we're advancing boost-glide and air-breathing systems to counter adversary developments like China's DF-17 and Russia's Kinzhal. Our solid rocket motor investments—including 3D-printed casings for 50% cost reduction—are feeding into the DoD's Hypersonic Multi-Service Air-Breathing Weapon and Operational Fires programs. Q2 highlights include a successful end-to-end test of our scramjet demonstrator achieving Mach 7 sustained flight, with thermal management via ceramic matrix composites we've scaled from F-35 production lines. This dual-use tech is also spinning into commercial hypersonic cargo concepts, eyeing partnerships with Blue Origin.

Space and resilient architectures at 20% or $2.1 billion: With the U.S. Space Force's Proliferated Warfighter Space Architecture accelerating, we're pouring resources into low-Earth orbit constellations for missile warning and comms. Our $450 million Q2 investment yielded the first orbital demo of our quantum-secured optical inter-satellite links, outperforming legacy RF by 10x in data throughput and jamming resistance. Regionally, this aligns with AUKUS Pillar 2 commitments, where we're collaborating with BAE Systems Australia on resilient PNT to deter Indo-Pacific aggression—a market we see growing at 15% CAGR through 2030 per Teal Group's forecasts.

Finally, autonomy, AI/ML, and directed energy at 15% or $1.6 billion: We're embedding edge AI into unmanned systems, with our Loyal Wingman UAV demonstrator now flying swarm tactics in live DoD exercises. High-energy laser prototypes hit 300 kW output this quarter, targeting counter-UAS roles akin to Raytheon's HELWS but scaled for naval platforms. These efforts are enhanced by our $200 million digital twin infrastructure, using NVIDIA GPUs for predictive simulations that have already de-risked 25% of our CRAD milestones.

Strategically, this R&D portfolio is tailored to the FY2025-2029 Future Years Defense Program, where the DoD projects $145 billion in RDT&E—a 9% increase over the prior cycle. Regionally, 62% of our R&D is U.S.-centric via DoD primes, 22% international like F-35 Block 4 upgrades for NATO allies such as the UK and Japan, plus GCAP contributions with BAE and Mitsubishi, and 16% commercial dual-use, including sustainable aviation fuels R&D for Boeing 777X derivatives to tap the $1 trillion post-2030 civil market.

The payoff? Our IRAD-to-CRAD conversion rate hit 72% this year—well above the sector's 55%—driving a $15 billion backlog in next-gen awards. Risks include supply chain pressures on rare earths for hypersonics and potential sequestration under debt ceiling talks, but our $5.2 billion in SBIR/STTR partnerships with startups like Anduril and Hermeus derisks innovation pipelines.

In summary, these investments aren't just expense line items; they're our competitive moat, ensuring ASD leads the sixth-gen era and beyond.

To wrap up the financials, in Q2 we reported revenue of $8.2 billion, representing a 12% increase year-over-year. Our adjusted earnings per share were $2.45. We continue to maintain a strong balance sheet with $4.5 billion in cash and equivalents. Our guidance for the full year remains as just updated. We are actively managing our costs and investing in key growth initiatives. We are also focused on returning capital to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases.

Our specific financial highlights include: Gross Margin of 28.5%, up 150 basis points; Operating Income of $1.8 billion; Free Cash Flow of $850 million.

Looking forward, we see FY24 revenue at the high end of $19.2-20.0 billion, with Defense accelerating to 20%+ growth in H2 on LRIP ramps. Headwinds peak Q3 but abate into 2025 as supply chains normalize, per our vendor scorecards showing 70% on-time delivery recovery.

Operator:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press *1 on your telephone keypad. Our first question comes from Josh Smith with JPMorgan. Please go ahead.

Josh Smith:
Good morning. Can you provide more color on the revenue headwinds, particularly supply chain and how you're mitigating them going forward?

Alex Thompson:
Certainly, Josh. As John outlined, supply chain disruptions, especially titanium forgings from Ukraine and Russia-exposed sources, have increased costs by 40% and extended lead times to 18 months, similar to what we've seen in Boeing's 737 MAX challenges. Labor shortages at facilities in Oklahoma and Alabama limited capacity by 5%, and Boeing's production slowdowns created a $250 million OEM shortfall in commercial. We've mitigated this through diversification—70% of rare earths now sourced domestically—productivity bonuses to hedge wage inflation, and digital twins that cut unplanned downtime by 25%. Our vendor scorecards show 70% on-time delivery recovery, and we expect headwinds to peak in Q3 before easing in 2025. Our 1.25x book-to-bill and $145 billion backlog give us strong visibility.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Lisa Chen with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Lisa Chen:
Hi, thanks. I'm curious about the aftermarket and services growth—can you elaborate on the sustainability of that 22% YoY increase and regional breakdowns?

John Ramirez:
Lisa, great question. That 22% growth to $1.8 billion, now 35% of revenue, is highly durable, marking 11 straight quarters of double-digit gains thanks to our installed base and digital tools like Predictive Health Management on 4,500+ engines, boosting revenue per flight hour 18% and retention to 98%. Commercial aviation led at +28% to $1.1 billion, with APAC up 45% from IndiGo and AirAsia LTSAs worth $2.5 billion. North America +25%, EMEA +15%. Defense +15% to $600 million on F-35 and C-130J MRO, margins up 300 bps to 28% via additive manufacturing and our Integrated Sustainment Ecosystem. Space +35% on new hypersonic deals. Full-year outlook 20-23%, with $8 billion new wins and ASD Nexus adding $50 million in fees already. FX and shutdown risks exist, but 85% backlog visibility supports it.

Operator:
Our next question comes from Mark Rivera with Barclays. Please go ahead.

Mark Rivera:
Thanks. Regarding the updated revenue and earnings guidance—what's driving the raise, and how does R&D fit into the margin expansion?

John Ramirez:
Mark, the raise to $19.2-20.0 billion revenue and $9.20-9.80 EPS reflects better execution across segments. Commercial up to $6.8-7.2 billion on A-350X orders and air traffic at 105% of 2019; Defense to $8.7-9.2 billion on $25 billion backlog, NGAD, and hypersonics; Space to $3.7-4.0 billion on Artemis and LEO. Margins expand 150 bps to 14.5-15.5% from fixed-price mix, debt refi at 4.2%, and repurchases. R&D at $10.5 billion (4.7% of rev) is key—$4 billion on NGAD for Mach 2+ demos, $2.8 billion hypersonics with Mach 7 tests, $2.1 billion space quantum links, and $1.6 billion AI/HEL at 300 kW. 72% IRAD-to-CRAD conversion adds $15 billion backlog, de-risked by digital twins and SBIRs. It's our moat for FYDP's $145 billion RDT&E.

Operator:
Thank you. There are no further questions at this time.

Alex Thompson:
Thank you for your questions. In closing, I'm confident in our ability to navigate the current environment and deliver long-term value to our shareholders. We remain focused on our strategic priorities, operational excellence, and innovation across defense systems, commercial recovery, and space technologies.

Mike Chen:
Thank you for joining us today. This concludes our Q2 2024 earnings call. A replay will be available on our investor relations website shortly.

Operator:
This concludes today's conference call. Thank you for participating. You may now disconnect.
